abstract: A major problem facing the development of quantum computers or large scale quantum simulators is that general methods for characterizing and controlling are intractable. We provide a new approach to this problem that uses small quantum simulators to efficiently characterize and learn control models for larger devices. Our protocol achieves this by using Bayesian inference in concert with Lieb-Robinson bounds and interactive quantum learning methods to achieve compressed simulations for characterization. We also show that the Lieb–Robinson velocity is epistemic for our protocol, meaning that information propagates at a rate that depends on the uncertainty in the system Hamiltonian. We illustrate the efficiency of our bootstrapping protocol by showing numerically that an 8-qubit Ising model simulator can be used to calibrate and control a 50 qubit Ising simulator while using only about 750 kilobits of experimental data. Finally, we provide upper bounds for the Fisher information that show that the number of experiments needed to characterize a system rapidly diverges as the duration of the experiments used in the characterization shrinks, which motivates the use of methods such as ours that do not require short evolution times.

specification.problem: Bootstrap characterization and control-model learning of a larger quantum simulator (e.g. a 50-qubit Ising simulator) using a small trusted quantum simulator (8 qubits), combining Bayesian inference, Lieb-Robinson bounds for compressed simulation, and interactive quantum learning, with Fisher information bounds motivating long evolution times.

Circuit, measurement and numerical details are not given in the abstract and are assumed generically.

specification.initial_state: Assumed product state |0>^{\otimes n} (or a simple product state) on both the device and the simulator, per experiment.

steps.description: Draw a prior over Hamiltonian parameters x and choose an experiment (evolution time t, initial state, observable) adaptively from the current posterior.
Restrict the simulation to the light-cone region of the observable, using the Lieb-Robinson bound so that the 8-qubit simulator suffices to compute the likelihood.
Evolve the device under H(x) for time t and evolve the simulator under the candidate model for the same t.
Update the posterior with the measured data, and repeat until the posterior is sufficiently narrow. Long t is preferred because the Fisher information shrinks at short t.

specification.measurement: Assumed: after evolution for time t, measure the qubits in the light cone of the chosen observable in a fixed local basis (e.g. computational), repeating for a number of shots to estimate outcome frequencies. The abstract does not specify the basis or shot count; only the ~750 kilobit total data budget is stated.
specification.classical_postprocessing: Use the outcome record as the likelihood input to the Bayesian update (eq_1), with the likelihood computed on the 8-qubit simulator restricted to the light cone (eq_2). Select the next experiment adaptively from the posterior and stop when the posterior covariance is small. The final estimate is the posterior mean, whose precision is bounded by eq_3.
